title: How to Protect Indoor Air Quality During Wildfires
h1: How Can You Keep Indoor Air Clean During Wildfire Smoke?
description: When wildfire smoke rolls in, your home can still have cleaner air. Here is how to seal up, set your HVAC system correctly, and filter smoke out of the house.
quick_answer: Close windows and doors, set your HVAC to recirculate, and run the fan with the best filter your system can handle, ideally MERV 13. Add a portable HEPA purifier in the bedroom, avoid anything that adds indoor smoke like candles or frying, and change the filter once the smoke clears.
body:
Wildfire smoke is part of life in Southern California. Even when a fire is far away, Santa Ana winds can push smoke across San Diego and Orange County for days. The fine particles in that smoke get into homes easily, but with a few changes you can keep the air inside much cleaner than the air outside.

How does wildfire smoke get inside your home?

Smoke comes in through every gap: around doors and windows, through attic vents and recessed lights, and through leaky return ducts that pull air from the attic or garage. Older stucco homes with original windows tend to leak more.

The particles that matter most are called PM2.5. They're small enough to get deep into your lungs, and a basic fiberglass filter doesn't catch most of them. That's why smoke can linger inside long after it's cleared outside.

What should you do when smoke rolls in?

  1. Close up the house. Shut windows, doors and the fireplace damper. Keep pets inside so the door isn't opening constantly.
  2. Turn off fresh air intakes. If your system has an outside air damper or ventilator, close it or switch it to recirculate. Window and evaporative coolers should be off.
  3. Run the HVAC fan. Set the thermostat fan to "On" instead of "Auto" so air moves through the filter all day.
  4. Upgrade the filter. A MERV 13 filter catches most smoke particles. Check that your system can handle it, because some older systems lose too much airflow with a dense filter.
  5. Add a portable purifier. A HEPA unit sized for the room, running in the bedroom overnight, gives you one clean space to sleep.
  6. Don't add more smoke. Skip candles, incense, the gas stove where you can, and vacuuming without a HEPA filter.

Which filter is best for wildfire smoke?

For most central systems, a MERV 13 filter is the target. It captures a large share of fine particles without restricting airflow as much as higher ratings. A thicker media filter, 4 or 5 inches deep, holds more and lets air through more easily than a 1-inch filter with the same rating.

Keep a couple of spares on hand before fire season. During heavy smoke, filters load up quickly, so check yours every week or two and replace it when it's visibly gray. A clogged filter cuts airflow and makes your system work harder.

If you're not sure what your system can take, our indoor air quality team can check static pressure and recommend the right setup, including media filter cabinets and whole-home air cleaners.

How can you make one room a clean air room?

Pick a bedroom with few windows. Close it off, run a portable HEPA purifier sized for that room, and keep the door shut as much as possible. This is especially useful for kids, older adults, and anyone with asthma or heart and lung conditions.

Check the purifier's clean air delivery rate (CADR) for smoke and match it to the room size. Running it on a higher setting for a few hours before bed helps.

What should you do after the smoke clears?

  • Replace the HVAC filter, even if it hasn't been long.
  • Wipe down surfaces with a damp cloth and vacuum with a HEPA-equipped vacuum.
  • Air the house out once outdoor air quality is good again.
  • If ash got into the attic or the smell lingers in the ducts, consider a duct cleaning.

Smoke odor that hangs around for weeks is often sitting in duct liner, attic insulation or the filter cabinet. Cleaning those areas usually takes care of it.

Getting ready before fire season

The best time to prepare is late summer, before Santa Ana season picks up. Buy spare filters in your system's size, test your portable purifier, and check that windows and doors close tightly. Weatherstripping on exterior doors and sealing gaps around attic hatches cut down on how much smoke slips in. If your return ducts run through the attic and have loose connections, sealing them keeps the system from pulling smoky attic air straight into the house.
faqs: Should I run my AC during wildfire smoke?

Yes, as long as it recirculates indoor air and doesn't bring in outside air. Running the system pushes air through your filter, which removes smoke particles. Close any fresh air damper and keep windows shut.
Is MERV 13 too restrictive for my system?

Some older systems or undersized return ducts struggle with dense filters. Signs include weak airflow, a whistling return, or a coil that freezes. A technician can measure static pressure and suggest a deeper media filter that cleans well with less restriction.
Do air purifiers help with wildfire smoke?
Portable purifiers with true HEPA filters do a good job on smoke particles in the room they're sized for. Avoid units that make ozone, which irritates the lungs.
How do I get the smoke smell out of my house?
Change the HVAC filter, clean surfaces and soft furnishings, and run a purifier with an activated carbon stage. If the smell lingers, the source may be ducts or attic insulation that need cleaning.
